summary: Describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol extension that includes an Allocation Token in query and transform commands. The token is a credential authorizing a client to request allocation of a specific object from the server.

eli5.summary: A special ticket lets one buyer claim a particular domain name, and without the ticket the claim fails.

subtitle: A credential extension for authorizing allocation of objects in domain registries.

tldr.problem: Domain registries need a way to control who can allocate specific objects (like premium domains or auction winners) without relying solely on transfer authorization mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8495 extends the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) with an Allocation Token element that can be included in query and transform commands to authorize the allocation of a specific object.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now enforce allocation policies by requiring valid tokens for create and transfer operations, enabling auctions, pre-eligibility programs, and founder allocations.

today: RFC 8495 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. The Allocation Token extension is registered as an active EPP extension applicable to any TLD.

sections.title: The Problem of Controlled Allocation
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) is used by domain registries to manage domain registrations and other objects. EPP already has mechanisms for transferring sponsorship of objects (moving them from one client to another), but registries often need finer control: they want to allocate specific objects only to authorized parties.

For example, a registry might want to allocate a premium domain name only to the winner of an auction, or allocate a domain only to someone with pre-eligibility credentials, or allocate a founder's reserved domain only to the founder's company. Before RFC 8495, there was no standard way to encode this authorization in EPP commands. The Allocation Token extension fills this gap by allowing a server to require a credential token when a client requests to create or transfer an object.
sections.eli5: Registries want to say 'only this person can have this domain', but EPP didn't have a standard way to prove it. Now it does.

sections.title: What Is an Allocation Token
sections.content:
An Allocation Token is a credential passed in EPP commands to authorize the allocation of a specific object. It is represented in XML as an element named allocationToken:allocationToken with a string value, such as abc123. The exact format and generation of the token is left to server policy; the RFC does not mandate a specific format.

The key distinction is that an Allocation Token is different from authorization information (which authorizes transfers). The Allocation Token is used to control who can initially allocate an object, while authorization information is used to control who can transfer ownership later. A client does not manage or choose the Allocation Token; the server defines it and may pass it out-of-band to an authorized party (for example, sending it in an email to an auction winner).
sections.eli5: A token is like a secret code the registry gives out. It's not something you set yourself; the registry tells you what yours is.

sections.title: Using Tokens to Check Availability
sections.content:
EPP's <check> command asks the server if an object is available for registration. The Allocation Token extension allows a client to include a token in the check command. The server then returns availability information that reflects the token's validity: if the object requires a token and the supplied token matches, the server returns the object as available; if the token does not match, the server should return it as unavailable; if the object requires no token, the server may return it as available regardless.

This allows a registry to offer a check command that says 'with your token, this domain is available', guiding clients toward objects they can successfully allocate. The RFC provides detailed examples showing single and multiple domain checks with token validation at various stages.
sections.eli5: When you ask 'can I have this domain?', the registry checks if your ticket matches. If it does, it says 'yes'. If not, 'no'.

sections.title: Creating and Transferring with a Token
sections.content:
The real power of the Allocation Token appears in EPP's transform commands. When a client issues a <create> command to register a new object, it can include the Allocation Token in the extension. The server validates the token before creating the object. If the token does not apply to the object, the server returns error code 2201.

Similarly, the <transfer> command (which requests a change in sponsorship) can include an Allocation Token. This is particularly useful when a registry wants to allocate an existing object, held by the registry itself or by another client, to a new sponsor who possesses the token. The token authorization is in addition to the normal transfer authorization mechanism, so both must be satisfied.

Other EPP commands—<delete>, <renew>, and <update>—are not modified by this extension; tokens apply only to allocation scenarios (create and transfer).
sections.eli5: When you try to register a domain or take one over, you must give your ticket. The registry checks it. No ticket, no registration.

sections.title: Retrieving Tokens via Info Queries
sections.content:
An authorized client can request the Allocation Token for an existing object using the EPP <info> command. The client includes an <allocationToken:info> element in the request. If the client is authorized (according to server policy), the server returns the token in the response. If the client is not authorized, the server returns error code 2201. If the client is authorized but no token exists for the object, the server returns error code 2303.

This mechanism allows a registry to share tokens with authorized parties through EPP itself. For instance, an auction system could query the registry to obtain the token for a purchased domain, then pass that token out-of-band to the buyer.
sections.eli5: If you're allowed to see it, you can ask the registry for your ticket. If you're not allowed, the registry says no.

sections.title: Security Guidelines for Tokens
sections.content:
RFC 8495 notes that the Allocation Token itself is just a mechanism for passing credentials; the security properties depend on how servers define and manage tokens. The RFC provides six security recommendations for Allocation Token definitions:

Protection in transit and at rest: tokens should be treated as secret and protected both when transmitted and stored. Single use: ideally each token should be unique per object and per allocation operation, preventing token reuse. Limited lifetime: tokens should have an expiry, either embedded in the token itself (if generated by a trusted third party) or checked on the server side. Strong randomness: if unsigned, tokens should use strong random values to prevent guessing. Digital signatures: tokens generated by a trusted third party should be signed for authenticity. Encoding: signed XML tokens should be encoded (e.g., base64) to avoid server validation issues.

The extension itself does not introduce security considerations beyond those in the core EPP protocol; security depends on how servers implement these recommendations.
sections.eli5: Tokens are like passwords. Keep them secret, use them once, and don't let them work forever. The registry should be careful with them.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Protocol Status
sections.content:
RFC 8495 registers two items with IANA. First, it registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:allocationToken-1.0 for the Allocation Token extension. Second, it registers the extension itself in the Extensions registry for EPP, marking it as a Standards Track extension that applies to any TLD.

The extension provides both an <allocationToken:allocationToken> element for passing tokens in commands and responses, and an <allocationToken:info> element (an empty marker) for requesting tokens in info commands. The XML schema is included in the RFC, allowing implementations to validate EPP messages against it.
sections.eli5: The RFC officially tells the internet's registry of protocols: 'Allocation Token is a real EPP extension now, and here's how to recognize it.'
